papers.title: GPTSwarm: Language Agents as Optimizable Graphs
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2024)
papers.core_contribution: Represents a language-agent system as a computational graph whose nodes are agents and whose edges carry messages, then optimizes node prompts and graph connectivity with gradient-based procedures.
papers.methodology: A differentiable graph abstraction supports prompt optimization at nodes and probabilistic edge optimization; experiments cover MMLU, HumanEval, and GAIA, including both single-agent and collaborative graphs.
papers.key_results: On GAIA, GPTSwarm scores 18.45 average versus 9.70 for GPT-4-Turbo, a reported 90.2% relative improvement; its level scores are 30.56, 20.93, and 3.85 for Levels 1-3. HumanEval pass@1 rises from 77% to 89% after prompt/demonstration optimization. Collaborative MMLU edge optimization improves accuracy by 2.1% plus or minus 1.1 over five training seeds.
papers.key_results_location: Table 1 and Section 3.4 (GAIA); Section 3.3 (HumanEval); Section 3.1.2 (MMLU edge optimization)
papers.limitations: The authors state that GPTSwarm does not optimize the internal topology within a node and that scaling beyond 100 agents introduces communication and robustness challenges.
papers.math_foundations: Directed computational graphs, differentiable categorical edge selection, backpropagation through graph-level objectives, and topological execution of acyclic graphs.
papers.motivation: Inference from the framing: the authors care about turning hand-designed agent collaboration into an optimizable object, using the computational-graph analogy to make prompts and communication structure amenable to a shared learning objective rather than treating orchestration as fixed scaffolding.
papers.constraints_inferred: Inference: API expense and nondifferentiable language calls favor small benchmark graphs and surrogate gradient estimators. The acyclic topological execution also narrows the runtime problem: arbitrary retries, recovery, and cyclic state transitions are outside the demonstrated graph contract.
papers.key_decisions: Inference: choosing a graph abstraction makes topology and prompt parameters jointly addressable, but a general state-machine abstraction would have required explicit transition guards and failure semantics. Using GAIA, HumanEval, and MMLU supplies heterogeneous evidence, while the small graphs leave large-scale reliability unresolved. Treating edges probabilistically enables optimization, but it tests learned connectivity rather than fully specified production control flow.
papers.tried_and_discarded: The authors report that simple instruction-only prompt optimization seldom improved the original prompt and retain demonstration-based optimization for the clearer HumanEval gain; GAIA aggregation uses selecting the best answer rather than relying only on self-consistency.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: Inference: task performance must be sufficiently smooth with respect to prompt and edge perturbations for the surrogate optimization signal to rank graph changes. If that local signal is unstable, the computational-graph analogy does not yield dependable workflow optimization.
papers.relevance_reason: This is the clearest foundational formalization of agents as optimizable graphs. It also exposes a project-critical gap: a graph executable in production still needs explicit transitions, termination, retry, and error states; a topological node order alone is not a complete state machine. Its results establish existence of gains, not their likely magnitude under our estimand or in live deployments.

papers.title: A Dynamic LLM-Powered Agent Network for Task-Oriented Agent Collaboration
papers.core_contribution: Introduces DyLAN, a dynamic agent network that selects agents and communication paths during execution instead of using a fixed collaboration topology.
papers.methodology: The system instantiates a temporal feed-forward agent network, ranks agents through forward peer scores and backward importance propagation, prunes low-importance agents, and applies an early-stopping rule when answers stabilize.
papers.key_results: DyLAN achieves 82.9 HumanEval pass@1 versus 73.2 for the single-agent baseline, a 9.7-point gain, using 16.85 API calls on average. On WebShop it obtains 68.3 reward and 42.0 success versus 50.6 reward and 28.0 success for direct generation, using 24.85 API calls. Across the arithmetic tasks, DyLAN scores 35.7 versus 31.6 for a single agent; with complex prompts it scores 37.6 versus 34.1. The abstract reports gains of up to 25% on selected MMLU subjects.
papers.key_results_location: Abstract (MMLU); Table 2 (HumanEval and WebShop); Table 3 (arithmetic tasks)
papers.limitations: The authors note that code-agent consistency uses BLEU where human annotation could better measure individual contribution; the system combines only relatively simple agent selection and team-reformation operations; and an extreme majority of contradictory agents can degrade results.
papers.math_foundations: Temporal feed-forward networks, graph pruning, forward scoring and backward importance propagation, plus a two-thirds agreement stopping heuristic inspired by Byzantine consensus.
papers.motivation: Inference from the failure framing: the authors care about allocating collaboration effort only to agents that contribute to the current task, because fixed teams waste calls and allow irrelevant or conflicting agents to dominate.
papers.constraints_inferred: Inference: expensive API evaluation limits the breadth of agent-role and round-count searches, motivating online pruning and heuristic stopping. The two-thirds rule is operational rather than a proven Byzantine guarantee under LLM dependence.
papers.key_decisions: Inference: dynamic selection trades reproducibility for task adaptation; the temporal feed-forward restriction keeps credit assignment tractable but excludes arbitrary cycles. Benchmarking both success and API calls makes efficiency visible, whereas a success-only study would conceal the orchestration cost. The early-stop rule bounds runtime, but a production state machine would also need transitions for disagreement, tool error, timeout, and recovery.
papers.tried_and_discarded: A preliminary experiment with experts from different domains did not significantly improve performance, so the retained configuration uses the same prompt for agents. Alternative agent-ranking formulations are examined in the supplementary ablations, with the forward/backward contribution method retained.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: Inference: peer-assigned importance must correlate with marginal task contribution. If agents systematically reward persuasive but incorrect peers, pruning can amplify the wrong coalition rather than contain it.
papers.relevance_reason: DyLAN directly informs dynamic loop allocation, agent pruning, and stop conditions while reporting call costs. Its consensus-inspired containment rule should not be mistaken for a bound on effect magnitude or reliability under correlated agents.

papers.title: AgentSquare: Automatic LLM Agent Search in Modular Design Space
papers.core_contribution: Defines an automatic search method over modular LLM-agent designs, evolving and recombining planning, reasoning, tool-use, and memory modules rather than optimizing a monolithic prompt.
papers.methodology: The paper constructs a design space with four module types and 16 seed modules, applies module evolution and recombination, and uses an in-context performance predictor to avoid evaluating candidates predicted to be unpromising.
papers.key_results: Across six benchmarks, AgentSquare reports an average 17.2% improvement over the best human-designed agents. The stated modular space contains 16 modules across four categories and 1,050 possible assembled agents.
papers.key_results_location: Abstract and Section 4 (17.2% across six benchmarks); Section 3 design-space definition (four categories, 16 modules, 1,050 combinations)
papers.limitations: The authors describe the modular design space as a constrained, non-comprehensive subset rather than a one-size-fits-all agent space; search quality also depends on the accumulated modules and the accuracy of the performance predictor.
papers.math_foundations: Combinatorial modular search, evolutionary generation and recombination, and in-context surrogate performance prediction.
papers.motivation: Inference from the modular framing: the authors care about reducing dependence on expert-authored agent pipelines and making reusable agent components searchable, while keeping the search space interpretable enough to attribute improvements to modules.
papers.constraints_inferred: Inference: exhaustively running 1,050 agents across six benchmarks would be costly, so a learned in-context predictor is used as an evaluation filter. The predefined module interfaces impose a strong compatibility prior and exclude runtime policies not expressible as those four module types.
papers.key_decisions: Inference: modular search improves reuse and search tractability, but it shifts the boundary of innovation to the curated module library. A predictor reduces API cost, while prediction error can prematurely remove unusual high-performing designs. Aggregate benchmark gain supports breadth, but it does not identify whether topology, prompt, model, or budget is the causal driver for a new workload.
papers.tried_and_discarded: The ablations compare removing module evolution, recombination, or the performance predictor; the full combination is retained. A free-form unrestricted code search is not evaluated and is therefore not visible as an attempted alternative.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: Inference: the best useful workflows must be composable from the seeded module vocabulary and the predictor must preserve their rank. If the decisive behavior lies outside the module interfaces, the search cannot discover it.
papers.relevance_reason: AgentSquare supplies a concrete modular search baseline and a warning that a constructed library is not evidence about the prevalence of workflow types in live systems. Any uncertainty statement must target candidate-ranking performance, not a broader claim about agent quality.

papers.title: AFlow: Automating Agentic Workflow Generation
papers.core_contribution: Automates generation and iterative improvement of code-represented agent workflows using Monte Carlo tree search and accumulated execution experience.
papers.methodology: AFlow expresses workflows as executable code, proposes edits with an LLM, evaluates candidates, and uses Monte Carlo tree search plus execution feedback to balance exploration and exploitation over workflow variants.
papers.key_results: Across six datasets, AFlow reports a 5.7% average improvement over state-of-the-art baselines. Workflows built with smaller models outperform GPT-4o-based baselines while costing 4.55% as much in dollar-denominated inference expense.
papers.key_results_location: Abstract and ICLR 2025 proceedings summary; main experimental results in Section 4
papers.limitations: The authors state that prior automated methods still rely on manual initial setup; AFlow reduces but does not remove dependence on a manually specified operator space, task evaluator, and search configuration. Evaluation and search cost remain tied to repeated workflow executions.
papers.math_foundations: Monte Carlo tree search, upper-confidence exploration over workflow candidates, and execution-feedback-based program search.
papers.motivation: Inference from the emphasis on code and search: the authors care about moving workflow engineering from artisanal prompt wiring to executable, testable program synthesis, with measured feedback determining which orchestration patterns survive.
papers.constraints_inferred: Inference: expensive black-box LLM calls and sparse task scores rule out exhaustive program search, motivating MCTS and a bounded operator vocabulary. Code expressiveness is useful, but unrestricted code also expands failure modes and makes validation part of the true optimization problem.
papers.key_decisions: Inference: representing workflows as code permits branches and loops that static DAGs cannot express, but it requires explicit runtime semantics to be reproducible. MCTS allocates evaluations adaptively, while a fixed budget would be easier to compare statistically. Dollar cost makes deployment efficiency legible, but it is provider- and date-sensitive and should not substitute for token and call counts.
papers.tried_and_discarded: The paper compares the full MCTS-and-experience search with ablations that remove accumulated experience or simplify the search strategy; the complete search loop is retained. Further abandoned workflow languages are not visible in the primary paper.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: Inference: the benchmark evaluator must be informative enough that local code edits can be selected before search budget is exhausted. If scores are noisy or exploitable, MCTS optimizes evaluator artifacts rather than reliable orchestration.
papers.relevance_reason: AFlow is a direct baseline for automatic workflow synthesis. For this project, executable code still must be normalized into fully specified states, guarded transitions, terminal conditions, and failure recovery before results are attributable and reproducible.

papers.title: G-Designer: Architecting Multi-agent Communication Topologies via Graph Neural Networks
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 42nd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2025)
papers.core_contribution: Learns task-conditioned sparse communication graphs for multi-agent systems with a graph neural architecture instead of selecting a fixed topology.
papers.methodology: A variational graph autoencoder conditions topology generation on agent representations and a virtual task node, with a sparsity objective to remove redundant communication before agents solve the task.
papers.key_results: The paper reports 84.50% accuracy on MMLU and 89.90% pass@1 on HumanEval. On HumanEval, token use is reduced by up to 95.33% relative to compared multi-agent baselines, and under the reported adversarial setting accuracy drops by 0.3 percentage points.
papers.key_results_location: Abstract; detailed benchmark and efficiency tables in the main experiments section
papers.limitations: The evaluated topology generator is conditioned on benchmark task encodings and a fixed candidate-agent set; the authors do not claim that the learned topology space exhausts possible communication policies or runtime recovery behavior.
papers.math_foundations: Variational graph autoencoders, graph neural networks, latent adjacency sampling, task-conditioned representation learning, and sparsity regularization.
papers.motivation: Inference from the sparsity and adversarial experiments: the authors care about communication structure as both a cost bottleneck and an error-propagation channel, aiming to preserve useful collaboration while pruning redundant or harmful edges.
papers.constraints_inferred: Inference: differentiable graph learning requires fixed agent features, a trainable task representation, and benchmark feedback; those requirements exclude unseen runtime states that have no training analogue. Sparse topology also lowers tokens, which likely made efficiency a central design constraint.
papers.key_decisions: Inference: a virtual task node lets topology vary by query, whereas a static graph would test only one communication prior. Sparsity provides a controllable cost bias, but it can conflate fewer tokens with better topology. The adversarial test probes containment, yet a 0.3-point drop in that setup does not establish an upper bound on effect magnitude in other threat models.
papers.tried_and_discarded: Fixed fully connected, chain, star, and other hand-designed topologies are treated as baselines and lose to the learned design; the paper does not expose a broader set of abandoned topology-learning objectives.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: Inference: the task and agent embeddings must contain enough information to select useful edges before agents communicate. If decisive information appears only during execution, the precomputed topology can be systematically wrong.
papers.relevance_reason: This paper is the strongest learned-topology comparator and provides explicit efficiency and adversarial probes. Its graph is a communication design, not a complete loop controller: transitions, retries, termination, and error handling remain separate engineering objects.

papers.title: Multi-Agent Design: Optimizing Agents with Better Prompts and Topologies
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Multi-Agent System Search (MASS), a staged optimizer that treats local prompts, workflow topology, and global prompts as coupled design variables.
papers.methodology: MASS performs three conditional stages: block-level prompt optimization, topology optimization, and workflow-level prompt optimization. Candidate systems are searched under a maximum of ten agents and evaluated on held-out task sets with repeated runs.
papers.key_results: With Gemini 1.5 Pro, MASS averages 78.79 across eight tasks versus 70.26 for multi-agent debate and 69.72 for ADAS. With Gemini 1.5 Flash, MASS averages 74.30 versus 65.91 for multi-agent debate and 64.75 for ADAS. The experimental protocol caps candidates at 10 agents and evaluates final results over three runs.
papers.key_results_location: Table 1 (eight-task averages and baselines); Section 4 search protocol (10-agent cap and three evaluation runs); Table 2 (validation/test splits)
papers.limitations: The authors state that the topology space is not exhaustive, that even fully connected debate may contain redundant communication worth pruning, and that more advanced search is needed for sample efficiency.
papers.math_foundations: Staged black-box optimization over prompts and discrete workflow topology, conditioned search, and held-out empirical evaluation.
papers.motivation: Inference from the staged ablations: the authors care about the interaction between what agents say and who communicates, arguing that optimizing prompts or topology alone leaves material performance untapped.
papers.constraints_inferred: Inference: the ten-agent cap, held-out splits, and staged rather than joint search reflect black-box evaluation cost. Conditioning later stages on earlier choices reduces search complexity but makes results order-dependent and may trap the optimizer in an early local optimum.
papers.key_decisions: Inference: local-to-global staging makes a huge mixed search space feasible, while a joint optimizer could discover stronger interactions at greater cost. Eight tasks broaden external validity, but the constructed tasks do not estimate the prevalence of workflows in live traffic. Three-run summaries address run randomness only if uncertainty is stated for the same estimand, not for unseen domains or future model versions.
papers.tried_and_discarded: The appendix reports that reproducing AFlow with a different optimizer backbone was not a fair comparison because the meta-prompt did not transfer, and generated scripts sometimes entered infinite execution and timed out. These cases motivate controlled search operators and explicit termination checks.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: Inference: the staged factorization must preserve most prompt-topology interactions. If the optimal topology depends on prompts that only emerge after global optimization, the imposed search order can exclude the best system.
papers.relevance_reason: MASS is the most direct joint prompt-and-topology search baseline. Its infinite-script observation is especially important: executable workflows require total transition definitions and explicit terminal/error states before optimization can be trusted.

papers.title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
papers.core_contribution: Develops MAST, a process-level taxonomy of multi-agent-system failures grounded in annotated execution traces, and tests targeted interventions against recurrent coordination problems.
papers.methodology: The authors analyze more than 1,600 traces from seven systems, construct the taxonomy from 150 traces, annotate 14 failure modes in three categories, measure inter-annotator agreement, and test role and orchestration interventions.
papers.key_results: MAST contains 14 failure modes in three categories and reaches Cohen's kappa of 0.88. Among reported frequencies, step repetition is 15.7%, failure to follow task requirements 11.8%, failure to recognize completion 12.4%, and reasoning-action mismatch 13.2%; incomplete, incorrect, and premature verification failures are 8.2%, 9.1%, and 6.2%. Role specification improves success by 9.4 points, and system-level changes with the same model improve success by at most 15.6 points. MetaGPT shows 60-68% fewer specification and inter-agent-alignment failures than ChatDev but 1.56 times as many task-verification failures.
papers.key_results_location: Abstract and Section 3 (trace count, taxonomy, kappa); Section 4 and failure-distribution tables (frequencies); intervention analysis in Section 5 (9.4 and 15.6 points); comparative analysis in Section 5 (60-68% and 1.56x)
papers.limitations: The authors state that MAST is not exhaustive, that failure labeling remains affected by present LLM judgment limits, and that the tested interventions do not resolve all failures; completion rates remain low in difficult settings.
papers.math_foundations: Qualitative taxonomy construction, trace annotation, Cohen's kappa agreement, frequency analysis, and controlled intervention comparisons.
papers.motivation: Inference from the process-level annotation: the authors care less about another aggregate leaderboard than about locating where collective execution breaks, because a final failure score cannot distinguish bad reasoning from bad handoffs, verification, or termination.
papers.constraints_inferred: Inference: manual trace annotation limits sample depth and forces a finite taxonomy; using seven constructed systems provides contrast but cannot estimate real-world failure prevalence. LLM-based judgments and selected traces also constrain which failures are observable.
papers.key_decisions: Inference: analyzing traces rather than only final answers exposes state-transition failures. Building the taxonomy on 150 traces makes expert annotation feasible but puts pressure on transfer to the remaining corpus. Reporting interventions with the same base model partially contains model confounding, yet the magnitude remains system- and task-specific.
papers.tried_and_discarded: Simple role specification and orchestration changes are tested as mitigations; they improve some outcomes but are insufficient, especially for completion recognition and verification. The paper does not claim a single universal repair.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: Inference: the annotated trace contains enough evidence to identify the causal failure step. If important hidden state or tool behavior is absent, taxonomic labels can describe symptoms while mislocating the mechanism.
papers.relevance_reason: MAST supplies the failure vocabulary needed to evaluate orchestration beyond final accuracy. Its completion-recognition, repetition, action-mismatch, and verification categories map directly to the transitions a fully specified executable state machine must make explicit.

papers.title: Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems
papers.core_contribution: Runs a broad controlled study of when multi-agent scaling helps or hurts and builds an empirical predictor linking task properties, model capability, agent count, and orchestration architecture to performance.
papers.methodology: The current revision evaluates 260 configurations across six benchmarks, five orchestration architectures, and three LLM families, then fits regression models to predict scaling outcomes and tests homogeneous and heterogeneous agent teams.
papers.key_results: Across 260 configurations, the cross-validated predictor reaches R-squared 0.373, rising to 0.413 with the Agent Capability Index. Relative performance ranges from plus 80.8% on a financial/decomposable task to minus 70.0% on a sequential task, and the predicted optimal architecture is selected correctly in 87% of cases. Centralized heterogeneous teams underperform the strongest homogeneous team by 12.6 percentage points, while decentralized heterogeneous teams gain 2.0 points, mostly from the stronger model.
papers.key_results_location: Abstract and main scaling-results section (260 configurations, R-squared values, plus 80.8%, minus 70.0%, 87%); limitations and heterogeneity analysis (minus 12.6 and plus 2.0 points)
papers.limitations: The authors report that cluster-robust inference leaves only capability saturation statistically robust at the chosen alpha; experiments use at most nine agents; heterogeneity analysis contains 13 configurations; prompts are not tuned per architecture; only six benchmarks are used; and SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench subsets contain 20 tasks because of cost.
papers.math_foundations: Empirical scaling regressions, cross-validation, task-property interaction terms, cluster-robust inference, and a derived Agent Capability Index; the contribution is predictive empirical modeling rather than a universal causal theorem.
papers.motivation: Inference from the interaction analysis: the authors care about replacing the slogan that more agents are better with conditional decision rules, because task decomposability, sequential dependence, architecture, and baseline capability jointly determine whether coordination pays.
papers.constraints_inferred: Inference: the 260 configurations are large for API experiments but sparse relative to all task-model-topology combinations, which motivates pooled regression and coarse task descriptors. Cost-driven task subsets and a nine-agent ceiling limit tail behavior.
papers.key_decisions: Inference: a factorial configuration study supports interaction estimates that isolated benchmark demonstrations cannot. Cross-validation targets prediction within the sampled design distribution, not live prevalence or causal transport to future models. Architecture selection accuracy is decision-relevant, but its uncertainty must be stated for architecture choice under the sampled tasks rather than as uncertainty about universal scaling laws.
papers.tried_and_discarded: Heterogeneous model mixing is tested as a presumed route to complementary strengths; centralized mixing loses 12.6 points to the strongest homogeneous system, and the small decentralized gain is attributed mainly to the stronger model, so heterogeneity is not retained as a general scaling prescription.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: Inference: the selected task descriptors must capture the effect modifiers that determine scaling. If an omitted property drives both architecture choice and outcome, the predictor can fit sampled configurations while giving the wrong rule on new workloads.
papers.relevance_reason: This is the strongest empirical warning against topology-independent scaling claims. It distinguishes directional containment from effect magnitude: an architecture may reduce error propagation without guaranteeing a positive net effect, and estimates must match the task and decision estimand.

papers.title: MASEval: Extending Multi-Agent Evaluation from Models to Systems
papers.venue: Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, System Demonstrations (ACL 2026)
papers.core_contribution: Provides a trace-first evaluation library that treats the full multi-agent system, including framework defaults and runtime behavior, as the unit of analysis rather than attributing outcomes only to the language model.
papers.methodology: MASEval standardizes setup, execution, trace collection, evaluation, and reporting across three models, three frameworks, and three benchmarks, yielding 27 configurations while preserving each framework's native prompts, tool mounting, and error handling.
papers.key_results: Across 27 configurations, the mean performance range across models is 14.2 percentage points with standard deviation 7.5, versus a 12.4-point range across frameworks with standard deviation 6.5. On MACS Travel with Claude Haiku 4.5, smolagents scores 90.4 while LlamaIndex scores 59.5, a 30.9-point framework gap. In one GPT-5-mini smolagents trace, the agent retries the same clarification tool up to 23 times. The library reduces interface code by 83-91% and total evaluation code by 35-57%.
papers.key_results_location: Table 2 and Section 4.2 (27 configurations, model/framework ranges, 30.9-point example); qualitative trace analysis (23 retries); implementation comparison section (83-91% and 35-57% reductions)
papers.limitations: The authors emphasize inherent stochastic noise and focus on aggregate rather than pairwise conclusions. Framework defaults are intentionally not aligned, so the estimated framework effect is the system as shipped, including prompts, tool exposure, and error handling, rather than an abstract topology effect.
papers.math_foundations: Factorial comparative evaluation, descriptive dispersion across model and framework factors, reproducible trace schemas, and aggregate system-level reporting.
papers.motivation: Inference from preserving framework defaults: the authors care about the practical system a user actually runs, arguing that evaluation which swaps only model names misses orchestration behaviors that can be as large as model effects.
papers.constraints_inferred: Inference: aligning every framework component would be both labor-intensive and contrary to the product-level estimand, so the study accepts coupled implementation differences. Three frameworks, models, and benchmarks provide a balanced matrix but not live-usage prevalence.
papers.key_decisions: Inference: keeping native defaults estimates framework-as-shipped performance; harmonizing prompts and tools would instead estimate a narrower runtime-engine effect. Trace-first collection makes retries and failure states observable, while score-only evaluation would hide the 23-call loop. Aggregate comparisons reduce stochastic overinterpretation, but uncertainty still must be attached to the intended model/framework/task estimand.
papers.tried_and_discarded: No abandoned framework-normalization approach is reported; the authors intentionally reject forced behavioral alignment in favor of preserving native execution semantics.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: Inference: native defaults are a meaningful and reproducible representation of each framework. If defaults drift rapidly across versions, the framework comparison becomes a dated configuration comparison rather than a stable platform effect.
papers.relevance_reason: MASEval directly addresses orchestration confounding and observability. It demonstrates why model, framework, prompt, tool mounting, error handling, and retry policy must be recorded as one executable configuration before claiming a result.

papers.title: Agentic Harness Engineering: Observability-Driven Automatic Evolution of Coding-Agent Harnesses
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an automatic harness-improvement loop built around component, experience, and decision observability so edits are explicit, evidence-backed, predicted, evaluated, and revertible.
papers.methodology: Every editable harness component is represented as a file; trajectories are distilled into a layered corpus; each proposed edit includes a prediction manifest; evaluation outcomes update evidence; unsuccessful changes can be rolled back over iterative benchmark rounds.
papers.key_results: Across ten iterations, Terminal-Bench 2 pass@1 rises from 69.7 to 77.0, compared with 71.9 for the cited Codex baseline. On the AHE-hard subset, AHE scores 53.3 versus 56.7 for Codex. On 500 SWE-bench tasks, the evolved harness scores 75.6% using 461,000 tokens versus 75.2% using 526,000 tokens for the seed harness. Self-attributed regression predictions achieve 11.8% precision and recalibration predictions 11.1%, versus random baselines of 5.6% and 5.4%.
papers.key_results_location: Table 1 (Terminal-Bench 2, ten iterations, AHE-hard); Table 2 (SWE-bench score and tokens); decision-observability analysis (11.8%, 11.1%, 5.6%, 5.4%)
papers.limitations: The authors limit evaluation to Terminal-Bench 2 and SWE-bench; the operating point is fitted to GPT-5.4-high, confounding portability; self-modification guardrails are incomplete; and the implementation is a prototype.
papers.math_foundations: Iterative black-box optimization, structured attribution via prediction manifests, empirical calibration and precision analysis, trajectory compression, and rollback-based engineering control.
papers.motivation: Inference from the three observability pillars: the authors care about making self-improvement inspectable and falsifiable. A harness edit is useful only when one can see what changed, why the system expected it to help, what trajectories support it, and whether the next evaluation confirmed the prediction.
papers.constraints_inferred: Inference: million-token trajectories exceed practical review context, so layered distillation is necessary but lossy. Sparse benchmark feedback and expensive evaluations motivate ten coarse rounds and prediction tracking rather than fine-grained causal experiments for every edit.
papers.key_decisions: Inference: file-level components bound the mutation surface and make rollback reliable, whereas opaque prompt blobs impede attribution. Prediction manifests turn each edit into a reviewable hypothesis, while outcome-only hill climbing would learn without accountability. Holding the model operating point relatively fixed improves harness attribution but limits portability.
papers.tried_and_discarded: The iterative loop rolls back or supersedes edits whose predicted gains do not materialize; the paper also compares against ACE and TF-GRPO-style optimization baselines. Exact discarded edits are preserved in the reported iteration history rather than summarized as a single winning recipe.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: Inference: the distilled experience corpus must retain the causal evidence needed to choose harness edits. If compression omits rare but decisive failures, observability becomes selective and the evolution loop can overfit visible symptoms.
papers.relevance_reason: This is the best practitioner-facing design for auditable orchestration optimization: explicit editable state, trace evidence, predicted effect, evaluation, and rollback. It also warns that a contained mutation loop does not by itself establish a large or portable effect.

papers.title: Adaptive Test-Time Compute Allocation via Constrained Policy Optimization
papers.core_contribution: Formulates per-input test-time compute selection as a constrained policy problem, derives a Lagrangian solution with budget control, and learns a cheap policy that imitates the oracle allocation.
papers.methodology: For discrete compute levels, the method estimates per-instance utilities, solves a Lagrangian relaxation, binary-searches the multiplier using cost monotonicity, and trains a policy from cheap input features to imitate the resulting oracle choices.
papers.key_results: The method reports up to 12.8% relative improvement on MATH and 3-6 percentage-point gains over uniform allocation, with more than 91% oracle-policy imitation. Across the reported settings, oracle gaps are 0.004-0.014 and imitation rates are 0.912-0.985.
papers.key_results_location: Abstract (12.8% and greater than 91%); conclusion (3-6 points and greater than 91%); Table 5 (oracle gaps 0.004-0.014 and imitation 0.912-0.985)
papers.limitations: The authors assume discrete compute budgets and offline utility tables; continuous allocation, online adaptation, and multi-objective budgets remain open. The need for cheap predictive features leaves a gap between oracle and deployable allocation.
papers.math_foundations: Constrained stochastic policy optimization, Lagrangian relaxation, strong duality for the relaxed stochastic policy, monotonicity of expected cost in the multiplier, binary search, and a regret bound in which learned-policy regret is at most imitation error times the worst per-instance utility gap.
papers.motivation: Inference from the constrained formulation: the authors care about spending extra reasoning only where its marginal utility justifies the cost, replacing uniform round counts with a policy that respects a population-level budget.
papers.constraints_inferred: Inference: precomputing utilities at discrete depths makes the optimization and proof tractable but assumes stable offline estimates and a closed menu of loop depths. A general agent graph would add path-dependent states, communication cost, failures, and nonstationary utilities not represented in the table.
papers.key_decisions: Inference: stochastic relaxation enables strong duality and exact expected-budget control, whereas deterministic per-instance choices would create a harder combinatorial problem. Binary search exploits cost monotonicity and avoids generic constrained optimization. Imitation transfers the oracle to deployment, but its uncertainty concerns allocation-policy regret under the sampled utility table, not end-to-end workflow reliability.
papers.tried_and_discarded: Feature and policy ablations compare simpler linear or classifier variants with the retained allocation policy; unrestricted continuous budgets and online utility learning are deferred rather than attempted.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: Inference: the offline utility of each compute level must be accurate and sufficiently stationary for new inputs. If additional rounds have path-dependent or distribution-shifted value, the multiplier and regret guarantee no longer describe the deployed loop.
papers.relevance_reason: This supplies the cleanest theoretical starting point for allocating review or reasoning loops under a budget. Its guarantee contains regret under explicit assumptions; it does not bound the effect magnitude of arbitrary multi-agent orchestration, and extension to a graph requires fully specified state transitions and utilities.

papers.title: Towards Long-Horizon Agents: A Survey
papers.core_contribution: Formalizes a long-horizon agent as a base policy coupled to an external harness and organizes the field around externalized harness engineering and internalized model optimization.
papers.methodology: A 149-page survey and taxonomy spanning foundations, field evolution, six harness components, model optimization, five application classes, benchmarks, and four frontier axes.
papers.key_results: The paper defines three nested horizon levels (H1 intra-context, H2 cross-context, H3 cross-task), six external harness components (loops/workflows, context/memory, tools/skills, orchestration, hooks/middleware, verification), and nine frontier positions across evolution, effectiveness, efficiency, and trustworthiness. Its frontier explicitly calls for calibrated mid-run shortening, rerouting, stopping, early path-switching, safety-aware experience reuse, and independent invariant-preserving verification.
papers.key_results_location: Sections 2, 4, and 7; Table 8; official 149-page manuscript verified from the authors' GitHub/OpenReview-linked repository.
papers.limitations: Posted 17 July 2026 and not peer reviewed; it is a broad taxonomy rather than an empirical security study, and its frontier claims are positions rather than demonstrated solutions.
papers.math_foundations: Harness-coupled decision-process framing Agent = pi_theta plus H, with nested horizon/capability levels and trajectory-level objectives under resource and safety constraints.
papers.motivation: The authors argue that long-horizon competence cannot be attributed to model weights alone because runtime structure increasingly determines planning, state, recovery, verification, cost, and safety.
papers.constraints_inferred: Breadth forces the survey to synthesize heterogeneous evidence and leave many proposed frontiers at a conceptual level; rapid July-2026 publication means concurrent work may not be fully integrated.
papers.key_decisions: Separates externalized harness engineering from internalized optimization, treats their co-evolution as the central mechanism, and elevates budget-aware action plus governed autonomy to frontier axes.
papers.tried_and_discarded: Not reported as a design archaeology; the paper explicitly rejects equating long-horizon agency with merely long-running, autonomous, or self-evolving execution.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: The model-harness decomposition is stable enough to compare diverse agent systems, and long-horizon difficulty is meaningfully captured by nested intra-context, cross-context, and cross-task levels.
papers.relevance_reason: It directly validates the user's harness-to-loop-to-orchestration framing while crowding generic adaptive stopping; the remaining opportunity must be a sharper security-specific formulation with measurable adversarial value.

papers.title: AgentStop: Terminating Local AI Agents Early to Save Energy in Consumer Devices
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a lightweight supervisor that predicts low-probability-of-success trajectories and terminates them before more local-device energy is spent.
papers.methodology: Measures local agent power, thermal, battery, token, and time overhead, then uses low-cost execution signals including token log probabilities for predictive early termination.
papers.key_results: Reports 15-20% less wasted energy with less than 5% task-utility loss on web question answering and coding benchmarks.
papers.limitations: Efficiency-focused rather than adversarial; local consumer hardware and the chosen benchmarks do not establish security robustness or multi-agent transfer.
papers.math_foundations: Binary trajectory-success prediction under an energy-utility tradeoff.
papers.motivation: Iterative tool use and retries consume energy even on trajectories already unlikely to succeed.
papers.constraints_inferred: The supervisor must be substantially cheaper than the execution it prevents and tolerate some false early stops.
papers.key_decisions: Uses low-cost online signals and an explicit utility-loss bound rather than an expensive per-step judge.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: Log-probability and runtime signals predict eventual failure before the saved energy is spent.
papers.relevance_reason: It crowds a generic predictive-stopping contribution but does not address adversarially corrupted progress signals.

papers.title: Semantic Early-Stopping for Iterative LLM Agent Loops
papers.core_contribution: Stops iterative writer-critic loops using semantic-change and quality-improvement signals, with deterministic termination and paired replay evaluation.
papers.methodology: Generates a complete trajectory once, replays multiple stopping rules over identical drafts, caches judge calls, and separates operational from evaluation tokens.
papers.key_results: On 60 HotpotQA questions, the judge-free policy reduces operational tokens by 38% at parity quality (Delta Information Score -0.004, p=0.81); the quality-gated version is counterproductive, while the best-round oracle gains 0.115 over practical policies.
papers.limitations: Single-author preprint, 60-question test, one writer-critic loop, and non-adversarial semantic signals; stopping is not the same as selecting the best prior round.
papers.math_foundations: Deterministic termination and well-definedness, paired replay comparison, and empirical rather than claimed contraction.
papers.motivation: A fixed iteration cap ignores whether answer meaning or quality is still changing.
papers.constraints_inferred: Any per-step quality check must save more tokens than it costs, and a completed trajectory is needed for strictly paired offline replay.
papers.key_decisions: Separates a judge-free deployable rule from an oracle and accounts for evaluator tokens independently.
papers.tried_and_discarded: The full quality-gated rule is retained as a negative result because judging overhead dominates its savings.
papers.load_bearing_assumptions: Semantic stagnation is a useful proxy for marginal answer value in this loop and remains stable enough under replay.
papers.relevance_reason: It directly crowds fixed-cap replacement and supplies a strong paired-replay protocol, while leaving adversarial progress poisoning and graph-level actions open.
